 After winning historic trifecta, Arizona Democrats could enact sweeping pro-voting agenda 
 By Yunior Rivas 
 November 20, 2026 
 Prefer us on Google 
 to see more of our voting rights news coverage when you search.
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on Twitter 
 Share on Bluesky 
 Arizona Democrats will enter 2027 controlling the governor’s office and both chambers of the Legislature for the first time in six decades, giving the party something it has not had in generations: the power to turn its pro-voting agenda into law.
 Democrats won 37 of 60 seats in the state House and 20 of 30 in the Senate, while Gov. Katie Hobbs (D) and Secretary of State Adrian Fontes (D) both won reelection. Unlike a new majority starting from scratch, Arizona Democrats already have a lengthy list of election proposals waiting on the shelf.
 Fontes and incoming legislative leaders spent the past several years pushing proposals to restore permanent mail voting, expand voter registration, strengthen access for Native voters, invest in election infrastructure and create new state-level protections for voting rights only to watch them die under Republican control.
 While many of those now have a path to Hobbs’ desk, a unified government does not give Democrats unlimited power over Arizona’s election laws. Some of the state’s most consequential voting rules were approved directly by voters and can’t simply be repealed. Others are embedded in the state constitution, constrained by federal law or caught up in ongoing litigation.
 That leaves Arizona Democrats with two intertwined questions heading into their first legislative session in power: How aggressively will they use their new majority to expand voting in one of the country’s most competitive states — and how much can they actually change?

 Democrats already have a blueprint 
 One obvious starting point is the Voters First Act , a sweeping election package Fontes introduced in January alongside incoming Senate President Priya Sundareshan (D) and incoming House Speaker Oscar De Los Santos (D).
 It would create statewide vote centers, restore Arizona’s Permanent Early Voting List, extend early voting, require ballot-tracking and curing notifications, allow counting of certain ballots returned to the wrong county and invest more state money in cybersecurity and election infrastructure. It also called for Arizona to participate in the Electronic Registration Information Center (ERIC), a multistate voter-roll maintenance program.
 Alex Gulotta, Arizona state director for All Voting Is Local , a nonpartisan organization working to protect voting access at the local level, said vote centers are particularly valuable.
 “There’s really no reason not to have vote centers. They give voters the flexibility to go to a voting location that works for them instead of being locked into one specific precinct,” Gulotta said. “Without that flexibility, there can end up unacceptably long lines at some polling places.”
 One of the most immediate fights could be over Arizona’s early-voting list.
 Republicans in 2021 replaced the state’s Permanent Early Voting List with the Active Early Voting List (AEVL). Under the current system, voters who go two consecutive election cycles without using an early ballot can be removed from the list if they fail to respond to a county notice, meaning they will no longer automatically receive an early ballot by mail.
 Democrats have repeatedly sought to restore the old system.
 But the timing could complicate an otherwise straightforward repeal. County recorders are required to send the next round of AEVL notices on or before Jan. 15. The new Legislature convenes Jan. 11, leaving just days between Democrats taking power and the statutory deadline.
 Expanding registration — and access 
 Democrats are also likely to revisit broader changes to voter registration.
 Sundareshan introduced legislation this year that would have created both automatic voter registration and same-day registration. Under the proposal, eligible Arizonans could register during the 28 days before an election or on Election Day or when using Motor Vehicle Division services. 
 Those proposals would significantly change a state that currently closes regular voter registration 29 days before an election.
 That would also require Arizona to modernize its voter registration infrastructure, Gulotta said.
 “With a more modern system, you should be able to scan documents directly into the system, update a voter’s information and make those changes much more efficiently,” Gulotta said. “That creates a real pathway for things like same-day and automatic registration.”
 Democratic lawmakers have also spent years targeting restrictions they say disproportionately burden Native voters.
 Arizona Republicans enacted legislation in 2022 requiring voter registration applicants to provide proof of their location of residence, among other new registration requirements. Tribal voting advocates have argued that conventional address requirements can create particular difficulties on reservations, where some homes lack standard street addresses.
 “You can have somebody who has already proven they’re a citizen but then get denied their right to vote over proof of residence. That can disproportionately affect young voters, students and Native voters who may not have conventional address documentation,” Gulotta said. “A tribal ID can establish your citizenship, but it may not have a residential address on it.”
 Democratic lawmakers have separately proposed requiring counties to consult with tribal governments when selecting voting locations and expanding access to polling sites and ballot drop boxes on college campuses.
 The new majority could also revive a much more ambitious proposal: an Arizona State Voting Rights Act .
 Democratic senators introduced the legislation this year to create an independent state-law framework for protecting voting rights. Among other provisions, it would prohibit gerrymanders that dilute the voting strength of protected groups, expand language-access requirements and give private plaintiffs and the attorney general new enforcement tools. Sundareshan was among its co-sponsors.
 Unlike the Voters First Act, which focuses largely on how elections are administered, the Arizona State Voting Rights Act would create a broader legal framework for challenging discriminatory or burdensome voting practices.
 Whether leadership will make that bill a priority next year remains unclear. Democrats are no longer limited to blocking Republican election legislation. They now have to decide what a Democratic voting system should look like.
 A trifecta still has limits 
 However, the biggest check on Democrats’ ambitions may be Arizona voters.
 In 2004, voters approved Proposition 200, which required documentary proof of citizenship for state voter registration and identification before receiving a ballot at the polls.
 Because it was enacted by voters rather than lawmakers, Democrats cannot repeal it with an ordinary party-line vote.
 Arizona’s Voter Protection Act prevents the Legislature from repealing voter-approved laws outright. Amendments generally must further the purpose of the original measure and receive support from three-fourths of each legislative chamber.
 So voting rights advocates are looking at ways lawmakers could strengthen protections around the existing citizenship requirements without simply repealing Proposition 200.
 Gulotta pointed to the 2018 LULAC consent decree , which established protections for certain registration applicants caught between Arizona’s documentary proof-of-citizenship rules and federal registration requirements.
 “One thing the Legislature can do is codify the protections that came out of the LULAC consent decree, so those protections aren’t just dependent on litigation or a court agreement,” Gluotta said.
 Under the framework created through the litigation, some voters who cannot establish eligibility for Arizona’s full state ballot can still be registered to vote in federal elections.
 “There are people who are eligible to vote federally but get pushed into this federal-only category because of Arizona’s additional document rules. We should make sure eligible voters can get a full ballot when they’ve already established their eligibility,” he said.
 That highlights an important distinction between the portions of Arizona election law Democrats can rewrite and the voter-approved provisions they cannot simply repeal.
 Democrats could instead ask voters themselves to change protected laws or amend the state constitution, something they’ve already discussed . That would make voter rights much harder to unwind if Republicans gain control over the state in the future.
 Fontes has also signaled that Democrats should use their majority to dismantle Republican policies like voter-registration restrictions, a ban on private funding for election administration and limits on third-party ballot collection.
 Those fights could reveal how far Democrats are willing to go beyond restoring older rules.
 The 2028 clock is already running 
 Whatever Democrats decide, they will be writing election rules in one of the country’s most consequential presidential battlegrounds .
 Democrats cannot assume their trifecta will last. They won their legislative majorities after six decades out of power, and another election could again change control of either chamber. For most of Hobbs’ first term, Arizona’s voting rights debate centered on what Republican lawmakers could pass and whether the Democratic governor would veto it.
 Starting in January, the equation will be fundamentally different.
